newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Thistle Hotels sets slim premium on debut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thistle Hotels sets slim premium on debut.

text.p: Thistle Hotels on Wednesday made its debut on the London stock market in a flotation valuing London's biggest hotel group at more than a billion pounds.
The hotelier's shares swiftly set a slim premium to its 170 pence issue price as investors rushed to check in to the sale.
The price tag was announced by the group's major shareholder New Zealand's Brierley Investments Ltd, whose stake in Thistle falls to 46 percent from 70 percent after the float.

Thistle, formerly Mount Charlotte Group until it was taken over by Brierley in 1990, saw its shares trade around 172.5 pence in volume of more than 25 million shares, making it the most actively traded stock in London.
Thistle chief executive Robert Peel, who also headed the Mount Charlotte group before its takeover, said he was delighted the company had made its stock market comeback.
"The excellent response from retail investors gives us an exciting opportunity to develop their loyalty and custom going forward," he said in a statement.
A company spokesman said some two-thirds of the stock on offer had gone to British investors and one third overseas.

Thistle raised some 237.6 million pounds ($372.1 million) through the offering, which gave it a market value of some 1.05 million pounds ($1.64 million), at the bottom of the indicated range for the float.

The price was pegged at the bottom of a 170 to 210 pence range initially set by Brierley because of fears that a rush by British hotel companies to list on the stock market would dull investors' appetite.

Hotel companies have been seeking stock market listings to capitalise on a recovery in British business and consumer demand after a lengthy downturn. Interest in the sector was given a further boost earlier this year by Granada Group's bid for Forte -- the country's biggest hotel group.

The flotation allows Brierley Investments to realise its aim of reducing its holding in Thistle below 50 percent. Thistle became the New Zealand conglomerate's biggest asset after the Mount Charlotte takeover and it was always understood that Brierley would want to cut its holding.
Brierley said the float had been priced at the bottom end of the range to ensure strong demand and a solid share register.
Spokesman Mike Drogemuller in Wellington said most of the top British institutions had supported the offer and Brierley considered it more important to get a good register.
"That reflects the lower price," he said, "It's important that the float gets away positively."
He said a slide in Brierley's shares from a recent high of NZ$1.44 showed investors expected Thistle to float at the bottom of the price range. Brierley's shares closed two cents lower at $1.37.
Analysts said Thistle had looked expensive at the upper end of the price range.

"The general perception was that it was quite an expensive offering on measures such as cash flow, historic return on capital and normalised earnings before depreciation and tax," said Fraser Ramzan, analyst at Lehman Brothers.
Thistle's main focus is in the four-star hotel market. The group has 100 hotels in total, including 24 in London and 25 in Scotland.
